locator: Chapter 2, Section 2.3.2 and Table 2-9 Historical Annual ADD, MDD, Peak Day, and Peaking Factor, printed p. 2-11 (PDF p. 76); Executive Summary ES.2, printed p. ES-5 (PDF p. 29); Table ES-1, printed p. ES-6 (PDF p. 30)
shows: The City of Auburn's 2024 Water System Plan (May 2025) gives the average day demand (ADD) and the maximum day demand (MDD) of the City for each year from 2015 to 2022, from its production and purchase records. The ADD is the annual supply divided by the days in the year. The MDD is the highest production and purchase in one day of the year. The highest MDD in Table 2-9 is 12.56 mgd on August 25, 2016. The highest MDD from 2017 to 2022 is 12.43 mgd on July 29, 2020, when the ADD was 6.32 mgd and the printed peaking factor was 1.97. The ratio of 12.43 to 6.32 is 1.9668 (derived). In 2022 the MDD was 11.78 mgd and the ADD was 6.56 mgd.
limits: The figures include the water that the City sold to other systems: sales to Algona in every year, and in 2015 and 2016 regular sales of about 300 MG a year to Lake Meridian Water District, which stopped in 2017. They also include the water lost from the pipes. The executive summary says that the MDD ranged from 11.25 mgd in 2019 to 12.43 mgd in 2020. This does not agree with the 12.56 mgd that Table 2-9 gives for 2016, and the plan does not explain the difference. The 2024 retail MDD of 12.47 mgd in Table ES-1 is a projection with a conservative planning value, not a record. The utility reports these figures itself, in a plan that its consultant prepared.

locator: Chapter 2, Section 2.2.2.1 Historical Wholesale Consumption, printed p. 2-6 (PDF p. 71); Table 2-6, printed p. 2-8 (PDF p. 73); Section 1.6.1.2, printed p. 1-21 (PDF p. 62); Section 3.4.1.2, printed p. 3-36 (PDF p. 141); Table ES-1, printed p. ES-6 (PDF p. 30)
shows: The plan names two wholesale water agreements of the City. Algona gets a firm (uninterruptible) supply under Agreement IA3A. Algona's use averaged 0.33 mgd from 2015 to 2017 and 0.36 mgd from 2018 to 2022. Table 2-6 gives 132.07 MG for Algona in 2020, which is 0.3608 mgd over 366 days (derived), and 125.29 MG in 2016. Lake Meridian Water District (LMWD) bought 302.89 MG in 2015 and 303.02 MG in 2016. It stopped regular purchases in 2017, and its agreement now allows interruptible sales up to 2.5 mgd. The agreement of Covington Water District (CWD) ended. Neither district bought wholesale water in the planning period. The supply analysis leaves out the demand of the Muckleshoot Indian Tribe's planned fish hatchery, which is not built. Table ES-1 projects Algona at 0.365 mgd on an average day and 0.692 mgd on the maximum day of 2024.
limits: Table 2-6 gives each customer's annual use in million gallons; the daily average is derived. The plan does not give Algona's use on the City's maximum day. The agreement lets the City cut Algona's supply by the same percentage as a failure of its own supply. The LMWD intertie can still carry water when LMWD asks for it, so the sales on one day can be more than the regular sales.

locator: Chapter 3, Table 3-19 Supply Analysis with Largest Source Out of Service and its notes, printed p. 3-36 (PDF p. 141); Table 2-12, printed p. 2-16 (PDF p. 81); Section 3.1.2.1, printed p. 3-15 (PDF p. 120)
shows: Table 3-19 of the plan gives the supply of the City in the 2024 scenario. Its total of 15,610 gpm is Wells 1, 2, 4, 5, 5A and 6 (7,955 gpm), Coal Creek Springs (3,500 gpm), West Hill Springs (600 gpm) and the two Tacoma interties (3,555 gpm). The City's own wells and springs give 12,055 gpm (derived), which is 17.36 million gallons a day. The 2024 maximum day demand in the same table is 8,657 gpm. Table 2-12 gives a pumping or production capacity of 13,140 gpm for the active wells and springs. Wells 3A, 3B, 5B and 7 are offline. The sources have chlorination and corrosion-control treatment, not a central treatment plant.
limits: These are source capacities in the City's planning analysis, not tested rates. Coal Creek Springs gives 3,500 gpm as its typical production limit, and its flow changes with the aquifer. Table 2-12 lists 9,040 gpm for the six active wells (derived) and Table 3-19 gives 7,955 gpm; the plan does not explain the difference. A note to Table 2-12 says that the new Well 2 pump gives 1,115 gpm, not the 1,600 gpm in the table. The Tacoma interties are water bought from another system, not a source of the City.

locator: Chapter 3, Section 3.1.4 Storage Facilities, printed p. 3-20 (PDF p. 125); Table 3-7 Inventory of Storage Reservoirs, printed p. 3-21 (PDF p. 126); Table 3-29 System-Wide Storage Analysis for the 2024 Scenario, printed p. 3-45 (PDF p. 150)
shows: The plan says that the City has 15.7 MG of water storage in eight reservoirs. Table 3-7 lists Reservoir 1 (5.0 MG), Reservoir 2 (3.6), 4A (1.0), 4B (1.5), 5 (1.0), 6 (1.0), 8A (1.2) and 8B (1.5), which sum to 15.8 MG (derived). These are maximum tank volumes. The storage analysis in Table 3-29 gives a maximum storage capacity of 15.86 MG for the retail water service area in 2024. It deducts 0.28 MG for the reserve share of Algona and 1.50 MG of dead storage, which leaves 14.08 MG of usable storage.
limits: The plan gives three totals for the same eight reservoirs (15.7, 15.8 and 15.86 MG) and does not reconcile them; they differ by the rounding of tank volumes. The City usually operates the reservoirs below their maximum levels, so the stored water at one time is less than these capacities. Planning capacities, not measured volumes.

locator: Chapter 1, Section 1.6.1.1 City of Tacoma, printed p. 1-17 (PDF p. 58); Chapter 2, Section 2.3.1 and Table 2-7 Historical Annual Water Supply by Source, printed p. 2-10 (PDF p. 75); Section 2.6, printed p. 2-16 (PDF p. 81); Section 8.2.3.1.1, printed p. 8-9 (PDF p. 221)
shows: The City can buy water from the City of Tacoma through two wholesale interties. A 2014 agreement gives a total of 3.5 mgd of average use and 5.12 mgd of peak use from the two interties together. The B Street NW intertie can carry up to 2,200 gpm and the 132nd Avenue SE intertie up to 4,500 gpm. Their combined use cannot be more than 5.12 mgd (3,555 gpm) in 24 hours. Table 2-7 shows purchases of 732 MG in 2015 and 321 MG in 2016, and none from 2017 to 2022. The plan says that the City has not bought water from Tacoma since 2016. It counts the interties as a source in its supply analysis. Through Cascade Water Alliance, the City also has 3.32 mgd more supply on the peak day and 1.5 mgd on an average day.
limits: The 3.5 and 5.12 mgd are contract limits, and 2,200 and 4,500 gpm are the limits of the connections. They are not water that flows in normal operation. Whether Tacoma can send the water during an emergency depends on its own supply.
